qs.q: An adolescent presents with chronic bloody stools, crampy abdominal pain, weight loss, and oral ulcerations. What is the definitive diagnostic procedure for confirming inflammatory bowel disease?
qs.e: Colonoscopy allows direct visualization and biopsy of the mucosa to diagnose inflammatory bowel disease such as Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis. Stool cultures are used primarily for infectious etiologies of diarrhea rather than chronic inflammatory conditions.

qs.q: Which of the following genetic factors is specifically highlighted in the pathogenesis of inflammatory bowel disease?
qs.e: NOD2/CARD15 is explicitly recognized as a genetic factor contributing to inflammatory bowel disease. Other genetic markers like HLA-B27 are not mentioned in this context.

qs.q: Which autoimmune liver condition is characterized by progressive obliterating fibrosis of both intra- and extra-hepatic bile ducts and is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease?
qs.e: Primary Sclerosing Cholangitis involves progressive obliterating fibrosis of intra- and extra-hepatic ducts and occurs in 75% or more of cases in association with IBD. Primary Biliary Cirrhosis primarily affects intrahepatic bile ducts alone.

qs.q: A 20-year-old female with a history of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) develops new onset of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Which symptom is most indicative of IBD over IBS?
qs.e: Rectal bleeding is a hallmark symptom that differentiates inflammatory bowel disease (like ulcerative colitis) from irritable bowel syndrome, which typically does not involve bleeding.

qs.q: Persons with inflammatory bowel disease have ulcerating bowel lesions with a TH17 immune response extending over decades. Which cell type is mediating the tissue injury?
qs.e: TH17 is a subset of helper T lymphocytes that produce IL-17, promoting neutrophil recruitment and chronic mucosal inflammation. T lymphocytes are the primary mediators in this cell-mediated (type IV) chronic inflammatory bowel response.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) comprises ulcerative colitis and Crohn's disease, chronic immune‑mediated disorders causing relapsing gut inflammation. Diagnosis relies on endoscopy, imaging, and histology, while management balances inflammation control, nutrition, and complication prevention.

sections.p: IBD includes two main phenotypes: ulcerative colitis (continuous colonic mucosal inflammation) and Crohn's disease (transmural, segmental inflammation that may affect any GI tract portion). Diagnosis requires endoscopic visualization with biopsies showing chronic inflammatory changes, plus imaging to assess extent.
b: Endoscopy with biopsies is the gold standard.
Radiologic imaging (CT/MR enterography) defines disease location and complications.

t.b: Confirms diagnosis and distinguishes ulcerative colitis from Crohn's; histology shows crypt architectural distortion, granulomas (Crohn's).
Screens for intestinal inflammation; high levels suggest active IBD vs functional IBS.
Maps small‑bowel disease and detects strictures, fistulas; essential for Crohn's staging.

sections.p: Severity guides therapy. Ulcerative colitis uses the Mayo score; Crohn's uses the CDAI and endoscopic indices. Staging also incorporates complications such as strictures, fistulas, or extra‑intestinal disease.
b: Mayo 0‑3: remission to severe colitis.
CDAI <150: remission; 150‑220 mild; >450 severe.

sections.p: IBD results from a dysregulated immune response to gut microbiota in genetically susceptible hosts, triggered by environmental factors.
b: Genetic predisposition (NOD2, IL23R).
Microbial dysbiosis.
Smoking (worsens Crohn's, may protect ulcerative colitis).
Infections common in low‑resource settings (e.g., TB, HIV) can mimic or trigger flares.

sections.p: Patients report chronic abdominal pain, diarrhea (often bloody in ulcerative colitis), weight loss, and fatigue. Extra‑intestinal signs include arthritis, skin lesions, and hepatic sclerosing cholangitis.
b: Ulcerative colitis: bloody diarrhea, urgency, tenesmus.
Crohn's disease: abdominal pain, non‑bloody diarrhea, perianal disease.

sections.p: Beyond endoscopy, labs and imaging help assess activity, complications, and rule out mimics.
b: CBC, CRP, ESR for systemic inflammation.
Serologies (ASCA, pANCA) aid phenotype but not diagnostic.

t.b: Detects anemia or leukocytosis; anemia may indicate chronic blood loss or malabsorption.
Quantifies inflammatory burden; high CRP suggests active disease.
Excludes infectious colitis when diarrhea is acute.

sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and require urgent care.
b: Toxic megacolon (colonic dilation >6 cm with systemic toxicity).
Perforation, massive hemorrhage.
Severe malnutrition, fistulas, strictures causing obstruction.

sections.p: Therapy aims to induce remission, maintain it, and prevent complications. Choice depends on severity, location, and extra‑intestinal disease.
b: 5‑ASA (mesalamine) for mild ulcerative colitis – topical anti‑inflammatory.
Corticosteroids for moderate‑severe flares – rapid control, avoid long‑term use.
Immunomodulators (azathioprine, methotrexate) for steroid‑sparing maintenance.
Biologics (anti‑TNF, anti‑integrin, anti‑IL‑12/23) for refractory disease – target specific cytokine pathways.
Surgery for complications or refractory disease; colectomy cures ulcerative colitis.

sections.p: Regular monitoring detects relapse, medication toxicity, and cancer risk.
b: Annual colonoscopic surveillance after 8‑10 years of disease (or sooner with primary sclerosing cholangitis).
Vaccinations (influenza, pneumococcal, hepatitis B) especially when immunosuppressed.
Nutritional support and bone health monitoring.

sections.p: Several conditions mimic IBD clinically or endoscopically.
b: Infectious colitis (Shigella, Campylobacter, TB).
Ischemic colitis.
Irritable bowel syndrome (functional).

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely reassuring.
b: Normal fecal calprotectin does not exclude mild disease.
Negative ASCA/pANCA does not rule out IBD.
Endoscopic appearance may be normal in early Crohn's; imaging is needed.

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of toxic megacolon (distension, tachycardia, hypotension)

faq.a: No cure exists; treatment controls inflammation and prevents complications.

faq.q: Why does smoking affect Crohn's differently than ulcerative colitis?
faq.a: Smoking worsens Crohn's by promoting immune activation, while nicotine may reduce colonic inflammation in ulcerative colitis.

faq.q: Is colon cancer risk higher in IBD?
faq.a: Yes, especially after 8‑10 years of extensive colitis; regular surveillance colonoscopy is recommended.
